title: Sophie E. Weides
text:
Research
I study how alpine and arctic plants respond to climate change, so which species are moving upslope, which are not, and what happens to plant communities because of these shifts. My PhD at the University of Basel takes a European-scale view of this by combining resurveyed historical vegetation plots all across Europe to which I added with my fieldwork in Norway and Svalbard.
Before Basel I spent five years at the University of Tübingen doing my Bachelor and Master. During my thesis I asked a different kind of question: where, exactly, do grassland plants get their water from? Using stable isotopes, I traced roots to their water sources and found that plants partition the soil more reliably than drought models tend to assume.

title: Outreach
text:
FameLab Basel 2023

  
  

Where does the water come from? This was my talk at the FameLab Basel 2023 semi-final — a science communication competition where the constraint is the point. You only get three minutes and no slides, so the brevity forces you to decide what actually matters.
The talk was about the topic of my master thesis, which tried to answer the question from which depth meadow plants take their water and how they deal with drought and an increasing competition for a limited resource.

title: Outreach
section: Evening tours at the Botanical Garden of Basel
text:
Evening tours at the Botanical Garden of Basel
Since 2022 I have led public evening tours at the Botanical Garden of the University of Basel — the Feierabendführung series, which runs after work and is open to anyone. No background in botany required.

  Wurzelwelten - Von Atemwurzeln zu wandernden Bäumen
  
    Die Führung Wurzelwelten hat einen Einblick in die erstaunliche Vielfalt und Anpassungsfähigkeit von Wurzeln gegeben. Von Varankerung zur Wasser- und Nährstoffaufnahme bis hin zu Speicherung, Symbiosen und Kommunikation. Anhand von Beispielen wie Sumpfzypresse, Mangrove, Tillandsie, Orchideen, Efeu und Alraune wurde gezeigt, wie unterschiedlich Pflanzen ihre Wurzeln nutzen und an extreme Lebensräume angepasst haben. 
  



  Mythen, Magie, Medizin - Ethnobotanik im Wandel der Zeit
  
    In dieser Führung haben wir gesehen wie eng Pflanzen seit jeher mit Heilkunst, Ritualen, Mythologie und kulturellem Wissen verbunden waren. An Beispielen wie Aleo vera, Pfeffer, Tollkirsche, Kakao und Chinarinde wurde deutlich, wie sich die Bedeutung von Pflanzen zwischen Medizin, Magie, Kolonialgeschichte und moderner Kommerzialisierung wandelte. 
  
  
    
      Event page ↗
    
  



  Botanische Intrigen: Parasitismus im Pflanzenreich
  
    Botanische Intrigen hat die faszinierende Welt parasitischer Pflanzen beleuchtet: von Misteln und Sommerwurzen bis zu raffinierten Halbparasiten wie dem Klappertopf. Die Führung hat gezeigt, wie Pflanzen einander anzapfen, sich dagegen wehren und warum Parasitismus in der Natur oft komplexer ist, als es auf den ersten Blick scheint.
  



  Heil- und Giftpflanzen
  
    In dieser Führung habe ich einen Einblick in die Welt pflanzlicher Gifte gegeben und gezeigt wie deren Wirkung von Dosis, Aufnahmeweg und Organismus abhängt. An den Beispielen von Tollkirsche, Fingerhut, Herbstzeitloser und Eisenhut wurde deutlich, wie Pflanzen Gifte als Schutzstrategie einsetzen und welche Bedeutung daraus für die Medizin und unsere Geschichte und Kultur wurde.

title: Outreach
text:
Fieldwork in Svalbard

  
  

A photo diary from fieldwork on the Svalbard, more exactly the Isfjorden, which is one of the northernmost places where vascular plants still grow. The trip is part of the data-collection work behind my PhD: resurveying historical vegetation plots to track how alpine plant communities have shifted as the Arctic warms. The Polarsteps log is a way to share the landscape, the logistics, the everyday life and of course the plants themselves with anyone curious about what fieldwork in the High Arctic actually looks like.

title: Research
text: I am interested into work across all spatial scales, from mountain ranges over elevational gradients to site specific experimental settings. The questions I find most interesting tend to be ones where the obvious answer turns out to be wrong.

title: Research
section: PhD: Arctic and alpine plants in a changing environment
text:
PhD: Arctic and alpine plants in a changing environment
Europe-wide redistributions of mountain plants during the Anthropocene
University of Basel · 2022 – present
Supervisors: Prof. Sabine Rumpf (Basel) · Prof. John-Arvid Grytnes (Bergen)
Zurich–Basel Plant Science Center
Alpine plants are moving upslope. That much is well established. What is less clear is why some species move and others don’t, whether the whole community shifts together or falls apart, and what actually sets the boundaries of where a plant can live. My thesis tackles these questions from three directions.
What actually determines the range limits of alpine plants?
Temperature is the usual suspect, but the evidence is patchier than the textbooks suggest. A systematic review I led, published in Ecology and Evolution (2026), synthesised what is actually known about the biotic and abiotic factors that set elevational range limits. The answer is much messier and more interesting than “it’s just too cold at the top”.
Do alpine plant communities becmome more similar and does everything happen all at once?
When species shift upslope at different rates, the composition of plant communities changes. While it is often assumed that the communities along the gradient become more similar it is still quite unclear how fast this process happens and which steps are involved. A chapter currently in preparation for Journal of Vegetation Science investigates this question further by using spatial scaling relationships and re-survey study spanning the last century.
Svalbard: Fieldwork on range shifts
As a guest PhD student at the University Centre in Svalbard (UNIS) with Prof. Philipp Semenschuk, I resurveyed historical vegetation plots in the Isfjorden area — sites that were first recorded decades ago, in one of the fastest-warming places on Earth. This work was funded by an Arctic Field Grant from the Research Council of Norway (100,000 NOK).

title: Research
section: MSc: Where does the water come from? Quantifying water-uptake depths of plants in changing grasslands
text:
MSc: Where does the water come from? Quantifying water-uptake depths of plants in changing grasslands
University of Tübingen · 2019–2021
Grassland plants growing side by side do not all drink from the same part of the soil. Using stable water isotope mixing models, I quantified how deep different species reach for water, and whether that changes when the grassland is subjected to strong experimental drought. The short answer: belowground niche partitioning is more resilient to drought than expected. The work became a first-author paper in Ecology (2024).
A companion study (Kramp et al., Ecology, 2022) showed the other side of the coin aboveground. While the partitioning itself holds, individual plant traits do shift: from tolerating drought to avoiding it altogether.

title: Research
section: BSc: Vegetation changes along grazing gradients in drylands
text:
BSc: Vegetation changes along grazing gradients in drylands
University of Tübingen · 2016–2019
My BSc thesis looked at how the functional composition of dryland plant communities changes along gradients of grazing intensity. Less a question about individual species, more about what types of plants can persist and which traits the environment is effectively selecting for.
